about.title: I’m curious about how things work. And how to make them better.
about.description: I’m Alena, a frontend developer with experience in backend development and testing. Today I focus on React, Next.js, and TypeScript. I enjoy building interfaces and understanding what happens behind them.

journey.title: From backend and testing to frontend
journey.description: My experience in backend development and testing shapes how I think about applications. Beyond appearance, I’m interested in data, error handling, and how the pieces connect. Frontend development lets me bring that experience to what people see and use on screen.

climbing.title: Away from code, I find routes on the climbing wall

projects.title: Selected projects and case studies
projects.description: This section will grow into a collection of projects showing React, Next.js, TypeScript, API integrations, and interface design in practice.

reserve.title: Reserve App
reserve.pitch: A full-stack app for future reservation management between trainers and clients. The current version presents authentication, a protected dashboard, API documentation, and a foundation for the reservation workflow.

items.label: Role
items.value: UI design, frontend implementation, API integration, and documentation of key technical decisions.

items.label: Goal
items.value: Build a solid foundation for a reservation app that can grow into time slots, bookings, roles, and administration features.

items.label: Focus
items.value: Authentication, protected pages, forms, data validation, API contracts, E2E tests, and full-stack deployment.

stack.title: Stack
items: React
Next.js
TypeScript
Zod
Tailwind CSS
NestJS
Prisma
PostgreSQL
Supabase

Vercel

done.title: What is done
items: Public landing page for introducing the app.
User registration and login through Next.js server actions and a NestJS API.
Protected dashboard available only after login.
User summary with data for the currently authenticated user.
Swagger documentation for the auth API and basic endpoints.
Playwright E2E test for login and dashboard rendering.
Web deployed to Vercel, API to Render, and database hosted on Supabase Postgres.

items.title: Frontend
items.description: The Next.js app includes a landing page, registration and login forms, a protected dashboard, and a placeholder for the future reservations overview.

items.title: API
items.description: The NestJS API handles registration, login, current user data, JWT authentication, input validation, and Swagger documentation. The reservation endpoint is still a prototype.

items.title: Data
items.description: The Prisma schema has the User model and roles in place. TrainingSession, Reservation, and notification models are planned as the next step.

items.title: Sign up and login
items.description: The user completes a form, data is validated, and the app works with an authentication token after a successful login.

items.title: Protected routes
items.description: Private areas check authentication state and prevent users from entering reservation or admin flows without a valid session.

items.title: Logout
items.description: Logout clears the client state and returns the user to the public part of the app without stale permissions.

testing.title: Testing and deploy
items: Playwright verifies the main completed flow: login, redirecting to the dashboard, and rendering the authenticated user data.
Swagger documentation is used to verify auth endpoints and request/response contracts.
Deployment is split between Vercel, Render, and Supabase Postgres.

learnings.title: What I learned
items: How to keep the contract between frontend and API consistent so backend changes do not break the user flow.
How to design an auth flow that feels understandable in the UI and remains safe at the route and data level.
How to present a technical project as a product story: problem, solution, implementation state, and next steps.

items.title: Reservation workflow
items.description: Add time slot selection, booking creation, and persistence of reservations in the database.

items.title: Reservation data model
items.description: Extend the Prisma schema with TrainingSession, Reservation, and user relationships.

items.title: Admin/trainer dashboard
items.description: Add availability management, reservation overview, and filtering by date.

jablonecSea.title: Jablonec Sea
jablonecSea.pitch: A mobile Expo app for quickly checking the current water and air temperature at the Mšeno reservoir in Jablonec nad Nisou. The project shows React Native UI work, an external data source, HTML parsing, loading states, and light/dark appearance modes.

items.label: Role
items.value: Mobile app design and implementation, data service, theme system, and tests.

items.label: Goal
items.value: Create a simple mobile overview of current reservoir conditions without making users search for the data on a website.

items.label: Focus
items.value: React Native UI, Expo Router, TanStack Query, parsing a public HTML source, error states, and testing.

stack.title: Stack
items: Expo
React Native
Expo Router
TypeScript
TanStack Query
AsyncStorage
Jest
React Test Renderer

done.title: What is done
items: Home screen with a card for the Mšeno reservoir.
Display of the current air and water temperature.
Data loading from the public Povodí Labe portal.
HTML table parser that finds the Mšeno reservoir row.
Loading, error, and retry states when the data source is unavailable.
Light, dark, and automatic appearance modes.
Persisted appearance preference using AsyncStorage.

items.title: Data source
items.description: The app reads a public Povodí Labe page and searches the table row for the Mšeno reservoir.

items.title: Parser
items.description: The service uses node-html-parser to turn HTML into a structure, normalize table cells, and map air and water temperature.

items.title: Fetching
items.description: TanStack Query handles loading state, five-minute cache, refetching on reconnect, and refetching when the app returns to the foreground.

items.title: Modes
items.description: The user can switch between light, dark, and automatic mode based on the system appearance.

items.title: Persisted setting
items.description: The selected appearance mode is stored in AsyncStorage, so it survives app restarts.

items.title: Themed components
items.description: Shared ThemedText and ThemedView components read current colors and keep the UI consistent across screens.

testing.title: Testing and quality
items: Jest tests verify the Mšeno parser, failed HTTP responses, missing rows, timeout handling, and network errors.
Home screen tests cover loading state, error retry, and rendering the reservoir card with data.
The project includes scripts for linting, type checking, test coverage, and CI checks.

currentWork.label: Currently working on
currentWork.title: Modernizing an installation wizard
description: I’m gradually migrating an installation wizard in an existing application from JavaScript to TypeScript.
I’m updating its forms, input validation, and API communication.
current: Moving to React Hook Form with Zod validation, integrating TanStack Query, and replacing Axios with the Fetch API.
The aim is to separate form state from server data and make error handling clearer.
next: I plan to generate an API client from the Swagger/OpenAPI specification.
I will standardize linting across the project.
I will write Playwright E2E tests for the installation wizard.
currentWork.context: Technical environment: a Java backend and a PostgreSQL database.

learning.title: Learning by doing
learning.description: I learn through hands-on practice. Here I share selected tutorials, videos, and small experiments — and what I tried along the way.

habitTracker.label: YouTube tutorial · Tried in practice
habitTracker.title: Habit Tracker
habitTracker.description: Following a tutorial, I built a habit tracking app with a weekly overview. Users can add habits, mark completed days, and browse previous weeks. Data stays saved in the browser after a page refresh.
habitTracker.learning: Sharing state with React Context, building a custom localStorage hook, and working with dates using date-fns. I also practised typing components and calculating daily progress.
habitTracker.intro: Following a YouTube tutorial, I built a daily habit tracker with React and TypeScript. This smaller project helped me practise shared state, custom hooks, and working with dates. Records are stored in the browser using localStorage.
features: Adding and deleting habits, with an empty-name check.
Marking and unmarking completion for individual days.
A Monday-to-Sunday overview and navigation through previous weeks.
A count of habits completed today and a streak calculated backwards from today.
Data persistence after refreshing the page in the same browser.
habitTracker.learningsTitle: What I practised and learned about

learnings.title: Shared state with React Context
learnings.description: HabitProvider manages habits and their operations. The form, list, and header access shared state through the useHabits hook.

learnings.title: A custom localStorage hook
learnings.description: The generic useLocalStorage hook loads stored data when initializing state and saves changes through useEffect. It falls back to the initial value when loading fails.

learnings.title: Dates stored as JSON
learnings.description: A Date object becomes a string when saved. I practised converting it back using a JSON.parse reviver and parseISO from date-fns.

learnings.title: Weeks and calendar days
learnings.description: I used date-fns for weekly intervals, week navigation, and calendar-day comparisons. The overview uses Czech day and month names.

learnings.title: State updates and derived values
learnings.description: Adding, deleting, and toggling completion create new arrays and objects using map, filter, and spread syntax. Daily progress and streaks are calculated from stored records.

learnings.title: Typed components
learnings.description: I practised typing habits, context, and component props. A shared button supports visual variants and standard HTML button properties.

next: Add habit renaming and use one consistent interface language.
Handle localStorage write failures and enable data export.
Adjust streak calculation to include a streak ending yesterday before today’s habit is completed.

ibuiltthis.title: I Built This — project directory
ibuiltthis.label: YouTube tutorial · Tried in practice
ibuiltthis.pitch: A platform for sharing and discovering projects with community voting. I built it following a Next.js 16 tutorial and practised connecting the interface, authentication, server actions, and a database.
ibuiltthis.intro: Through a YouTube tutorial project, I practised the journey from a form through input validation to storing and displaying data. It gave me a chance to explore the frontend and server side within one Next.js application.
features: A project directory with search and sorting.
Project detail pages with slug-based URLs.
A project submission form with input validation.
Voting and admin approval or rejection of submissions.
ibuiltthis.learningsTitle: What I practised and learned about

learnings.title: Server and client components
learnings.description: Separating server-side data loading from browser interactions. Project details use a dynamic slug route and generateStaticParams.

learnings.title: From a form to the database
learnings.description: Server Actions, Zod validation, and useActionState for submission status and feedback. Inputs are validated on the server before being saved.

learnings.title: Data modelling and PostgreSQL
learnings.description: Defining a schema with Drizzle ORM, migrations, and a Neon connection. I worked with unique slugs, indexes, and reading, inserting, and updating records.

learnings.title: Authentication and roles
learnings.description: Clerk integration, authentication checks for submissions and voting, and an admin role check on the admin page. I also tried working with organizations.

learnings.title: Caching and refreshing data
learnings.description: The cacheComponents setting, the use cache directive, dynamic loading with connection(), and revalidatePath after data changes.

learnings.title: React 19 interactions
learnings.description: Using useOptimistic and useTransition for voting, search state, and list sorting. I composed the interface from reusable components.

next: Check admin permissions inside the approval and rejection actions as well.
Track individual users’ votes and add feedback when voting fails.
Verify that all relevant views refresh after voting and moderation.
